candidate.title: Hittite Online, Lesson 1: Proclamation of Anittas (commentary on names and the god Siu)
candidate.venue: University of Texas at Austin, Linguistics Research Center
candidate.ask_addressed: Break the Indo-European thread into branch evidence: earliest attestation per branch (Anatolian)
candidate.quote: Although neither Anittas nor his father Pithanas bore an Indo-European name
candidate.summary: The commentary notes that the king and his father bore non-Indo-European names, while the god 'our Sius' (from PIE dyeus) points to an Indo-European cult, and suggests the Hittites were an ethnically mixed group.
candidate.limits: Commentary, not the text. It argues from one god-name and personal names; it does not show migration route or date of arrival.

strand.what: Hittite and a PIE sky-god cult in a mixed Hattic and Indo-European society

reason: strand_unsupported: the quoted sentence only says the names are non-Indo-European and a god 'might' be of Indo-European origin; it says nothing of a language or cult being carried into Anatolia, and the strand's dates and 'inferred' rating come from elsewhere

candidate.title: Indo-Aryan superstrate in Mitanni (treaty gods)
candidate.ask_addressed: Break the Indo-European thread into branch evidence: earliest attestation per branch (Indo-Aryan in the Near East)
candidate.quote: In a treaty between the Hittites and Mitanni
candidate.summary: Says the Suppiluliuma I and Shattiwaza treaty (c. 1380 BCE) invokes Mitra, Varuna, Indra and Nasatya, Indo-Aryan-looking names in Hurrian Mitanni.
candidate.limits: Wikipedia summary; the treaty tablet itself and Thieme 1960 were not opened. Shows Indo-Aryan-like names in the Near East by the 14th c. BCE, not a migration route or a Vedic date.

strand.what: Indo-Aryan divine names and horse terms
